Embarrassing home race
ATS founder Günter Schmid had commissioned
the development of his first Formula 1 car from
the remnants of the Penske and March F1 teams.
However, Robin Herd’s HS1 was, in 1978, miles
away from the modern wing cars at the front of
the field. To make matters worse, Goodyear had
stopped supplying the backmarkers with qualify-
ing tyres, making it impossible to finish in the top
12 in qualifying.
For ATS, the German Grand Prix at Hockenheim
was to offer no home advantage anyway: in qua-
lifying, Jean-Pierre Jarier had once again spun off
the track in the ATS due to a stuck accelerator
pedal. The Frenchman had enough now and left
the team that very Saturday evening.
Jochen Mass did qualify for the race on the hard
Goodyears, but started from the penultimate row,
with only Ertl and Stuck behind him. Whilst the last
cars were still rolling into their starting positions,
the race had already been given the green light at
the front. A chaotic start to the race.
The two idols of the German fans, Mass and Stuck,
returned from the first lap in only 20th and 21st
position and were absent from the second lap
altogether: in the fast Ostkurve of all places, the
ATS and the Shadow of the two Germans made
contact, and the race ended in the crash barriers
for both of them. An embarrassing home race for
ATS and a disappointment for the many fans.

The Art of Survival
Hardly any other Formula 1 car was repainted as
often over the course of just one season as the
1983 Arrows A6. The British racing team, led by
designer Tony Southgate and financier Franco
Ambrosio, suffered chronically from a severe lack
of funds. The powerful but expensive turbo engines
were simply out of reach, so they muddled through
from race to race with the Cosworth V8.
Sponsorship deals were often secured at the last
minute, and the A6 appeared at almost every
Grand Prix in a different livery, sporting the colours
of national sponsors. At the US Grand Prix, an over-
weight Alan Jones even made a one-off comeback,
but even that failed to attract a major sponsor.
Swiss driver Marc Surer was the only constant from
the start of the season, and from his home Grand
Prix at Spa onwards, the Belgian Thierry Boutsen
replaced the hapless Chico Serra. Meanwhile, the
sidepods were adorned with the logos of carpet
manufacturers, perfume brands, mint sweets and
Italian leather fashion.
At the penultimate race at Brands Hatch, it was
ultimately a London art gallery that made it
possible for the two Arrows cars to compete in
the European Grand Prix. A financially precarious
season had been weathered, but persevering had
paid off: from 1984, Barclays came on board as
the main sponsor, enabling the team to finally
switch to BMW turbo engines.

Turbos on a diet
The entire Formula 1 field lined up in 1986 with
1.5-litre turbo engines, but the reduction in fuel
consumption to 195 litres per Grand Prix was
causing headaches for the engineers and elect-
ronics specialists. At full power, the cars were at
risk of running out of fuel and breaking down be-
fore the race was even over. This prediction proved
accurate - particularly on the high-speed circuit at
Hockenheim.
Tyrrell had secured the fast Renault EF15 Turbo
V6 engines, which were retrofitted with pneumatic
valve control during the course of the year. A
supply of nitrogen compressed to up to 2,600 psi
now actuated the valves, thereby replacing the
inertia of the former valve springs.

In Data General, Ken Tyrrell had found an up-
and-coming American computer company that
financed the expensive turbo engines. This also
allowed him to circumvent the ban on tobacco ad-
vertising, which had already been in force at the
1986 German Grand Prix, amongst other events.
Martin Brundle had qualified the Tyrrell 015 in 15th
place and had already moved up to 9th before the
tyre changes.
However, on lap 25, a faulty electronics box sparked
a fire in the engine, leading to his retirement. The
real drama, however, unfolded at the very front of
the field: whilst running in second and third places,
the two McLarens driven by Prost and Rosberg ran
out of fuel just a few metres from the finish line.

Survivor &
The 1968 Grand Prix season marked a major
turning point in many respects: technical de-
velopment exploded, expensive titanium and
magnesium made their debut, and the door to the
world of aerodynamics was thrown wide open - a
Pandora’s box, as it turned out. Formula 1 became
immensely more expensive, and major sponsors
replaced the small stickers of the tyre and oil com-
panies.
The Cosworth V8 was no longer exclusively availab-
le to Lotus, but the greater loss for Colin Chapman
was the death of Jim Clark in a Formula 2 race at
Hockenheim, even before the European F1 season
had started. This made the then 39-year-old
Graham Hill the spearhead of the new Gold Leaf
Team Lotus for 1968.
Champion
The 1968 German Grand Prix at the Nürburgring
is still regarded today as the Formula 1 race with
the worst weather conditions. Continuous rain and
thick fog suggested the race should be abandoned,
yet the officials sent the drivers into the Green Hell
anyway. Jackie Stewart’s victory, with a lead of over
four minutes, remains the stuff of legend to this
day.
Graham Hill had to settle for second place, but took
the lead in the World Championship. With a victory
at the season finale in Mexico, the Briton was
crowned Formula 1 World Champion for the
second time after 1962, in a season in which mere
survival was a success. With Jim Clark, Mike
Spence, Ludovico Scarfiotti and Jo Schlesser, F1
had lost four big names in just one year.
